title: Food Culture and Nutritional Stratification: What You Eat and What It Means
body:
Food in GLMZ is one of the most legible markers of tier status, shaped by a combination of supply chain access, caloric subsidy programs, and the cultural meanings that have accreted around different modes of eating. The municipal Nutritional Subsidy Program, administered through the Corporate Civic Compact, provides Tier-4 and Tier-5 residents with monthly allocations of what are officially called 'Balanced Caloric Units' — gray zone-stable extruded protein and carbohydrate blocks produced in the Meridian Nutritional Manufacturing Complex in the South Industrial Ring. Colloquially, these are called 'slugs,' a term that began as slang and has become so universal that even official community nutrition workers use it without apparent irony. Slugs are nutritionally complete by regulatory definition and culturally associated with poverty so thoroughly that receiving them is experienced by many recipients as a stigmatizing act.

Mid-tier food culture in GLMZ is dominated by a form of cuisine that has evolved specifically within the megacity context: high-density vertical farming produce combined with cultured protein from the Great Lakes BioFarm Consortium, prepared in the modular kitchen formats common to Stack residential architecture. The Stack Kitchen — a 1.2-meter counter unit with an integrated induction surface, a small-batch fermentation chamber, and a recipe overlay interface — is the defining domestic appliance of Tier-3 life. Cooking from a Stack Kitchen has generated its own culinary tradition, emphasizing fermentation, pickling, and layered umami flavors that maximize the relatively narrow ingredient palette available through mid-tier distribution. Food culture publications like *Meridian Plate* and the neural-overlay cooking channel Ferment & Stack have built large audiences around this vernacular cuisine.

At the upper tiers, food functions as performance and network maintenance. Corporate dining culture along the Gold Corridor and in the Lakefront Executive District revolves around a handful of high-profile establishments that serve what is called 'provenance food' — ingredients with verifiable non-synthetic origin, often soil-grown outside the megacity and transported under cold chain protocols that make the food astronomically expensive. A single provenance dinner at Sable & Ferrite can cost more than a Tier-4 household's monthly caloric allocation. These meals are rarely about nutrition; they are about the demonstration of access, the performance of taste, and the social bonding that occurs when powerful people share something genuinely scarce.

The most complex food culture in GLMZ belongs to the immigrant and enclave communities who have maintained culinary traditions within the constraints of tier-limited ingredient access. In the Pilsen Mezzanine, a dense Tier-3 and Tier-4 mixed district with a large Central American heritage population, home cooks have developed techniques for replicating traditional dishes using Stack Kitchen ingredients and cultured substitutes. These adaptations are taken seriously as culinary art — the annual Pilsen Adaptation Table, a community food event now in its nineteenth year, showcases dishes that honor their origins while being entirely honest about their material constraints. Food writers from upper-tier publications periodically 'discover' this cuisine, generating a cycle of extraction, appropriation, and backlash that the community navigates with considerable fatigue and occasional dark humor.
